content: NIPA1, also known as Non-imprinted in Prader-Willi/Angelman syndrome region protein 1, is a protein encoded by the NIPA1 gene in humans. This gene is responsible for producing a protein that is believed to function as a transmembrane molecule, potentially acting as either a receptor or a transporter. Specifically, it is hypothesized that this protein may serve as a magnesium transporter. The NIPA1 protein is thought to play a critical role in the development and maintenance of the nervous system. While alternative splice variants of this gene have been identified, their precise biological roles remain unclear. Mutations in the NIPA1 gene have been linked to a human genetic disorder known as autosomal dominant spastic paraplegia 6. To investigate the function of NIPA1, model organisms have been utilized. A conditional knockout mouse line, named Nipa1tm1a(KOMP)Wtsi, was created as part of the International Knockout Mouse Consortium program. This initiative, conducted at the Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute, is a large-scale mutagenesis project aimed at generating and distributing animal models of human diseases for research purposes. Both male and female mice from this knockout line underwent a standardized series of phenotypic tests to assess the impact of the gene deletion. A total of 24 different tests were performed on the mutant mice; however, no significant abnormalities were detected in these animals.
